title: O, If Thy Brow, Serene and Calm
description: O, If Thy Brow, Serene and Calm in Tonic Solfa to CAITHNESS, doh is D: the solfa with the words, staff notation, 5 verses and a piano.
about: These words were printed without an author's name in A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion, compiled by Samuel Longfellow and Samuel Johnson (Boston, 1848), as hymn 287, “"Neither Do I Condemn Thee."”.
The book printed the words without tunes, marked Common Metre (8.6.8.6), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to CAITHNESS; any other Common Metre tune fits them as well.
underlay: O, if thy brow, se-rene and calm, From earth-ly stain is free, View not with scorn the err-ing one, He once was pure like thee.

lines: O, if thy brow, serene and calm,
From earthly stain is free,
View not with scorn the erring one, —
He once was pure like thee.
O, if the smiles of love are thine,
Its joyous ecstasy,
Shun not the poor forsaken one, —
He once was loved like thee!
And still, 'mid shame, and guilt, and woe,
One Being loves him still,
Who, blessing thee, hath poured on him
The world's extremest ill.
He knows the secret lure which led
Those youthful steps astray;
He knows that they who holiest are
Might fall from Him away.
Then, with the love of him who said
"Go thou, and sin no more,"
Save, save, the sinner from despair,
And peace and hope restore.

source: A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion (1848)
licence: Public domain: anonymous words in print by 1848.
credits: Words anonymous, public domain, as printed in A Book of Hymns for Public and Private Devotion (1848); set to CAITHNESS by NoteFusion, as words-only hymn books were sung.
